source.title: Information criteria as statistical complexity measures for AI models

record.file_problem: none; full article text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The article discusses double descent as a generalization phenomenon and cites prior work, but does not test any of the listed claim versions. Its numerical example compares several models on one simulated regression problem; it is not a sweep over model size, epochs, or sample size.
record.gate_note: The article mentions double descent in its discussion of learning-theoretic measures and leaves empirical comparison with double-descent diagnostics for future work. Section 5.6 reports held-out RMSE for six models with different stated complexity measures; these results bear on complexity and generalization but do not test a double-descent curve.
record.test_reason: Double descent is mentioned only in passing: two sentences, citing Belkin et al. as one of refs 10–12, plus a future-work note. The only numerical result is one simulated regression comparing six fixed models (Table 3). There is no sweep over model size, epochs, sample size, noise or regularization, and no risk curve around an interpolation threshold. The unpruned tree interpolates (75 leaves for 75 training points), but no model lies beyond that point, so no second descent can be observed.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that architectural size is not statistical complexity. They recommend reporting fit, complexity cost and residual uncertainty separately, using a criterion suited to each model class, rather than a single scalar.
record.recipe_differences: No double-descent reproduction or related intervention is performed.

fits_no_version.finding: Nominal or effective complexity does not order held-out RMSE across the six models. The unpruned 75-leaf tree, which interpolates, has test RMSE 0.5523. The depth-3 tree has 0.5519 and the degree-15 OLS polynomial has 0.4444.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In one simulated regression, model-class-specific complexity counts do not order held-out error, and an interpolating tree generalizes about as well as a shallow one.

record.problems: The numerical illustration is one simulated regression comparison with a 75-observation held-out set; no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are reported. It is not designed as a double-descent test.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise relevant Table 3 model results were left out.

untested.parts: All: no model-size sweep and no test-error curve around an interpolation threshold.
All: no epoch or training-time axis.
All: there is no capacity sweep. The interpolating unpruned tree is a single endpoint, with no models past the interpolation point.
All: no peak locations are measured on any axis.
All: noise level, multiple peaks and tuned regularization are not varied in relation to a peak. Ridge λ and Lasso α are fixed single values.
All: effective degrees of freedom are reported for ridge, but no double-descent curve is re-expressed against them.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'discusses' overstates the engagement: double descent appears only as a cited aside (Section 2.4) and as future work (Section 6), so the relation is changed to cites_only. All six rows correctly link to no version and are correctly marked cannot_determine. Table 3 has a single 75/75 split with no repeats or uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve around an interpolation threshold.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or risk curve past an interpolation point.
No peak locations measured along any axis and no test of whether one effective-complexity measure predicts them.
No test of label noise, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization in relation to a double-descent peak.
No double-descent curve is re-expressed against an effective parameter count.
